A fitted `gamlss2` model predicts the entire conditional response distribution.
Means, quantiles, and event probabilities can all be obtained from this
distribution through the same interface.

This vignette shows how to predict at new covariate values and construct
intervals. The main distinction is between a **confidence interval** for an
estimated quantity, such as the mean, and a **prediction interval** for an
individual future response. Model specification and fitting are introduced in
[First Steps](firststeps.html). We use the same ozone model as
[Bayesian GAMLSS](bayesian.html), fitted here by penalized likelihood.

## Data and model

We model daily ozone concentration in the `airquality` data using temperature
and wind speed. We reserve 20% of the complete observations for a simple
prediction check at the end.

```{r}
#| message: false
library("gamlss2")

air <- na.omit(airquality[, c("Ozone", "Temp", "Wind")])

set.seed(123)
i <- sample(nrow(air), floor(0.8 * nrow(air)))
train <- air[i, ]
test <- air[-i, ]

m <- gamlss2(
  Ozone ~ s(Temp) + s(Wind) | s(Temp),
  data = train,
  family = GA,
  trace = FALSE
)
```

The Gamma family `GA` has two parameters: `mu`, the conditional mean, and
`sigma`, the conditional coefficient of variation. Both use a log link.
The first right-hand side models `mu`; the second models `sigma`. Thus,
temperature can change both the mean and relative spread of ozone, while
wind enters the mean predictor.

## Predicting at new covariate values

Each row of `newdata` supplies the covariates for one prediction. Here we
consider temperatures of 65, 80, and 90°F at a wind speed of 10 mph.
The response is not required.

```{r}
weather <- data.frame(Temp = c(65, 80, 90), Wind = 10)
d <- predict(m, newdata = weather)
d
```

By default, `predict()` returns a vector of distributions using the
`distributions3` interface, one per row of `weather`. We can immediately
calculate means, quantiles, and probabilities.

```{r}
q <- quantile(d, probs = c(0.5, 0.9), elementwise = FALSE)

data.frame(
  weather,
  mean = mean(d),
  median = q[, 1],
  q90 = q[, 2],
  prob_above_80 = 1 - cdf(d, 80)
)
```

The median divides each fitted distribution in half; the 90th percentile is
exceeded with probability 0.1 under the fitted model. The last column gives
the probability of ozone exceeding 80 ppb, an illustrative threshold.
`elementwise = FALSE` evaluates both quantiles for every distribution:
rows correspond to `weather`, columns to the requested probabilities.

Other useful summaries are `sqrt(variance(d))` for the conditional standard
deviation and `cdf(d, 80) - cdf(d, 40)` for the probability of ozone between
40 and 80 ppb. These describe variation in the response, treating the fitted
parameters as fixed.

To compare the three temperatures over a range of ozone concentrations, plot
the density and the survival function. The height of each survival curve at
80 ppb gives the exceedance probability calculated above.

```{r}
#| label: distributions
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Fitted ozone densities (left) and exceedance probabilities (right) at three temperatures, with wind speed fixed at 10 mph."
#| fig-alt: "Three ozone density curves and their survival curves, with exceedance probabilities marked at 80 ppb."
wcol <- c("#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73")
yg <- seq(0.01, max(quantile(d, 0.995)), length.out = 500)
densities <- pdf(d, yg, elementwise = FALSE)
survival <- 1 - cdf(d, yg, elementwise = FALSE)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1), cex = 1)
matplot(yg, t(densities), type = "l", lty = 1:3, lwd = 2,
  col = wcol, xlab = "Ozone (ppb)", ylab = "Density",
  main = "Conditional density")
legend("topright", paste(weather$Temp, "°F"), col = wcol,
  lty = 1:3, lwd = 2, bty = "n")
matplot(yg, t(survival), type = "l", lty = 1:3, lwd = 2,
  col = wcol, ylim = c(0, 1),
  xlab = "Threshold (ppb)", ylab = "Exceedance probability",
  main = "Conditional survival function")
abline(v = 80, lty = 3, col = "gray50")
points(rep(80, nrow(weather)), 1 - cdf(d, 80), col = wcol, pch = 16)
par(op)
```

At higher temperatures, the fitted distribution shifts toward higher ozone
concentrations. Its shape also changes: at 90°F it is more concentrated around
its mean than at 80°F. Comparing only the means would miss this difference.

### Choosing the prediction scale

Use `type` to select the quantity returned by `predict()`.

| Call | Result |
|---|---|
| `predict(m, newdata = weather)` | Fitted response distributions |
| `predict(m, newdata = weather, type = "response")` | Conditional response means |
| `predict(m, newdata = weather, type = "parameter")` | A data frame of `mu` and `sigma` |
| `predict(m, newdata = weather, parameter = "mu", type = "link")` | Additive predictor for `mu`, here the log mean |
| `predict(m, newdata = weather, parameter = "mu", type = "terms")` | Individual contributions to that additive predictor |

Specifying `parameter` without `type` selects parameters on their natural
scale. For example, the following returns only `sigma`.

```{r}
predict(m, newdata = weather, parameter = "sigma")
```

For `GA`, `mu` is the mean, so `parameter = "mu"`, `type = "response"`, and
`mean(d)` agree. This is family-specific: `mu` need not be the response mean
in other families. Omitting `newdata` gives predictions for the fitted data.

## Confidence intervals

To see how the expected ozone concentration changes with temperature, we
construct a prediction grid and hold wind speed at its training median.
Supplying `level = 0.95` requests approximate pointwise Wald confidence
intervals.

```{r}
nd <- data.frame(
  Temp = seq(min(train$Temp), max(train$Temp), length.out = 100),
  Wind = median(train$Wind)
)

ci <- predict(m, newdata = nd, parameter = "mu", level = 0.95)
head(data.frame(nd, fit = ci$fit, lower = ci$lower, upper = ci$upper))
```

The result contains `fit`, `se.fit`, `lower`, and `upper`. For this model,
the bounds are calculated on the log-mean scale and transformed back, keeping
them positive. Each interval describes uncertainty in the mean at one temperature.
By default, the calculation holds the fitted smoothing parameters fixed.

### Smoothing-parameter uncertainty {#uncertainty-in-smoothing-parameters}

The degree of smoothness is itself estimated from the data. Use
`unconditional = TRUE` to include approximate uncertainty from this step.
Here, *unconditional* refers to the smoothing parameters; predictions remain
conditional on the supplied temperature and wind speed.

A vector of confidence levels requests several intervals in one call.
The bounds are then lists named by confidence percentage.

```{r}
ciu <- predict(m, newdata = nd, parameter = "mu",
  level = c(0.8, 0.95), unconditional = TRUE)
lower95 <- ciu$lower[["95%"]]
upper95 <- ciu$upper[["95%"]]
```

First compare the 80% and 95% intervals at each temperature. Then hold the
confidence level at 95% to see how much smoothing-parameter uncertainty
contributes to the width of the interval.

```{r}
#| label: confidence-intervals
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Pointwise confidence intervals for mean ozone at median wind speed, by confidence level (left) and treatment of smoothing uncertainty (right)."
#| fig-alt: "Nested 80 and 95 percent confidence bands on the left; conditional and slightly wider unconditional 95 percent bands on the right."
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1), cex = 1)
plot(nd$Temp, ciu$fit, type = "n", ylim = range(lower95, upper95),
  xlab = "Temperature (°F)", ylab = "Mean ozone (ppb)",
  main = "Confidence levels")
polygon(c(nd$Temp, rev(nd$Temp)), c(lower95, rev(upper95)),
  col = adjustcolor(wcol[1], 0.15), border = NA)
polygon(c(nd$Temp, rev(nd$Temp)),
  c(ciu$lower[["80%"]], rev(ciu$upper[["80%"]])),
  col = adjustcolor(wcol[1], 0.35), border = NA)
lines(nd$Temp, ciu$fit, col = wcol[1], lwd = 2)
rug(train$Temp, col = adjustcolor(1, 0.3))
legend("topleft", c("95%", "80%"),
  fill = c(adjustcolor(wcol[1], 0.15), adjustcolor(wcol[1], 0.35)),
  border = NA, bty = "n")

plot(nd$Temp, ciu$fit, type = "n", ylim = range(lower95, upper95),
  xlab = "Temperature (°F)", ylab = "Mean ozone (ppb)",
  main = "Smoothing uncertainty")
polygon(c(nd$Temp, rev(nd$Temp)), c(lower95, rev(upper95)),
  col = adjustcolor(wcol[2], 0.25), border = NA)
polygon(c(nd$Temp, rev(nd$Temp)), c(ci$lower, rev(ci$upper)),
  col = adjustcolor(wcol[1], 0.35), border = NA)
lines(nd$Temp, ciu$fit, lwd = 2)
rug(train$Temp, col = adjustcolor(1, 0.3))
legend("topleft", c("Conditional", "Unconditional"),
  fill = c(adjustcolor(wcol[1], 0.35), adjustcolor(wcol[2], 0.25)),
  border = NA, bty = "n")
par(op)
```

The 95% band is wider than the 80% band because it uses a higher confidence
level. Including smoothing-parameter uncertainty widens the 95% intervals
modestly in this example. The rug shows the training temperatures.

## Prediction intervals

A prediction interval describes the range of an individual future response.
The 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles enclose the central 95% of each fitted Gamma
distribution.

```{r}
dn <- predict(m, newdata = nd)
pi <- quantile(dn, probs = c(0.025, 0.975), elementwise = FALSE)
head(pi)
```

Equivalently, use `quantile(m, newdata = nd, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))`.
These prediction intervals treat the estimated model as fixed. Their coverage
on new data depends on how well the model describes the response distribution.

Overlay the two intervals at median wind speed. The distance between the
outer bounds shows how much daily ozone can vary even where the model
estimates the mean precisely.

```{r}
#| label: intervals
#| fig-cap: "95% prediction interval for daily ozone (gray) and pointwise 95% confidence interval for mean ozone (blue) at median wind speed."
#| fig-alt: "A wide gray prediction band and a narrower blue confidence band around the mean ozone curve over temperature."
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(nd$Temp, ciu$fit, type = "n", ylim = range(pi, lower95, upper95),
  xlab = "Temperature (°F)", ylab = "Ozone (ppb)")
polygon(c(nd$Temp, rev(nd$Temp)), c(pi[, 1], rev(pi[, 2])),
  col = "gray90", border = NA)
polygon(c(nd$Temp, rev(nd$Temp)), c(lower95, rev(upper95)),
  col = adjustcolor(wcol[1], 0.25), border = NA)
lines(nd$Temp, ciu$fit, col = wcol[1], lwd = 2)
rug(train$Temp, col = adjustcolor(1, 0.3))
legend("topleft", c("Prediction interval", "Confidence interval for mean"),
  fill = c("gray90", adjustcolor(wcol[1], 0.25)), border = NA, bty = "n")
```

### Including coefficient uncertainty

For quantities that combine several parameters, such as a response quantile,
coefficient draws provide a general way to propagate estimation uncertainty.
`FUN = identity` retains one vector of distributions per joint coefficient
draw. We evaluate the 90th percentile within each draw, then take quantiles
across draws to obtain an approximate confidence interval for that percentile.

```{r}
draws <- predict(m, newdata = weather, FUN = identity,
  R = 2000, seed = 1328, unconditional = TRUE)
q90 <- sapply(draws, quantile, probs = 0.9)
bounds <- t(apply(q90, 1, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975)))

data.frame(weather, q90 = quantile(d, 0.9),
  lower = bounds[, 1], upper = bounds[, 2])
```

Rows of `q90` correspond to prediction locations and columns to coefficient
draws. This calculation accounts for uncertainty in both `mu` and `sigma`,
including their dependence. The bounds describe uncertainty in the 90th
percentile; they are not a range containing 95% of future responses.
The same approach works for an event probability, evaluated within each draw
as `1 - cdf(d, 80)`.

To include coefficient uncertainty in a prediction interval, generate
responses from each draw's distribution and take quantiles of the pooled
responses. For the second weather scenario:

```{r}
set.seed(1329)
y <- unlist(lapply(draws, function(d) random(d[2], 100)))
quantile(y, c(0.025, 0.975))
```

For Bayesian fits, `predict()` uses stored posterior draws. The same
construction gives posterior predictive intervals; omit
`unconditional = TRUE`. See [Bayesian GAMLSS](bayesian.html) for posterior
summaries and diagnostics.

## Checking predictions {#observations-held-out-from-fitting}

We now predict for the held-out days using each day's own temperature and
wind speed, and check how often ozone falls inside its prediction interval.

```{r}
pt <- quantile(m, newdata = test, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
inside <- test$Ozone >= pt[, 1] & test$Ozone <= pt[, 2]

data.frame(
  n = nrow(test),
  coverage = mean(inside),
  mean_width = mean(pt[, 2] - pt[, 1])
)
```

Judge coverage alongside interval width: very wide intervals may cover well
while offering little useful precision. This small test sample gives only a
rough check. For forecasting later observations, use a time-ordered split
instead of the random split used here. [Forecasting and Assessment](topmodels.html)
introduces calibration plots and scoring rules.

For your own prediction data, include covariates from all parameter predictors
and any offsets, preserve the training factor levels, and check whether the
covariate combinations are represented in the fitting data. Predictions use
the modeled response scale: if the response is `log(y)`, exponentiating
quantiles gives quantiles of `y`, but exponentiating the mean does not give
the mean of `y`.

The help topic `?predict.gamlss2` documents further options;
`?vcov.gamlss2` describes the covariance choices. For profiles that vary one
covariate while fixing the others, see `?marginal_predict`. The distribution
interface and the distinction between family parameters and response means
are developed further in [Family Objects](families.html) and
[Family Extensions](family_extensions.html).
